title: "Capstone Prep: what each rubric section is asking for"
format: html

The capstone is graded on **8 sections, 100 points, pass at 60** — with one
extra rule: **no single section may score below 40% of its points.** A strong
project cannot compensate for a section you skipped.

This page maps each section to the lesson that teaches it, states what full
marks looks like, and names the mistake that most often costs the points.
Everything in the "commonly lost on" column is a pattern seen repeatedly in
real submissions.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read this first
Most lost marks are **not** from difficult work done badly. They are from a
requirement nobody noticed — a deliverable that was never attempted, or one
that was written about but never actually run. Go through this table before you
start, and again before you submit.
:::

## The eight sections

### 1. Agent fundamentals — 15 pts

**Where:** [Agents](01_agents.ipynb) · [Sub-agents](02_subagents.ipynb)

**Full marks:** real tool calls the model chooses to make, plus structured
output (`with_structured_output` + a Pydantic model) wherever the result is
parsed by code rather than read by a human.

**Commonly lost on:** returning a hardcoded f-string from a "tool" instead of
doing real work. If the function ignores its arguments, it is not a tool call.

### 2. Multi-agent / routing architecture — 15 pts

**Where:** [Sub-agents](02_subagents.ipynb) ·
[Customer support agent](08_customer_support_agent.ipynb)

**Full marks:** the routing decision is made by the **LLM** — a supervisor that
classifies with structured output, or a real handoff — matching one of the four
track patterns.

**Commonly lost on:** `if "email" in question.lower():`. Keyword matching is
not routing. It is the single most frequent architecture mistake, and it is
visible in one glance at the code.

### 3. RAG pipeline — 15 pts

**Where:** [RAG overview](03_retrieval.qmd) · [Embeddings](04_embeddings.ipynb)
· [Semantic search](05_semantic_search.ipynb) · [RAG agent](06_RAG_agent.ipynb)

**Full marks:** documents genuinely loaded → split → embedded → stored →
retrieved, **and** a written justification of 2-Step vs. Agentic vs. Hybrid RAG
for *your* problem.

**Commonly lost on:** a retriever that returns nothing. Ask a question whose
answer is verbatim in your documents; if the answer says *"the context does not
contain that information,"* your pipeline is broken no matter how correct the
code looks. In a notebook this is usually cells run out of order — restart the
kernel and run top to bottom before believing anything.

### 4. Context & state management — 15 pts

**Where:** [Context and state](07_context_and_state.ipynb) ·
[Long-term memory](12_long_term_memory.qmd)

**Full marks:** a checkpointer with a `thread_id` for short-term state, **and a
separate Store** for long-term facts — with a cross-thread test proving a fact
written in one thread is readable from a different one.

**Commonly lost on:** calling a growing list of chat messages "long-term
memory." The rubric explicitly rules this out. If your long-term memory
disappears when the thread changes, it was short-term memory.

### 5. Human-in-the-loop — 10 pts

**Where:** [Customer support agent](08_customer_support_agent.ipynb) ·
[Thinking in LangGraph](09_langgraph.qmd) · [Reliability](13_reliability.qmd)

**Full marks:** a real `interrupt()` that pauses before something
irreversible, **and** a `Command(resume=...)` that completes the run — both
demonstrated, both with output in the notebook.

**Commonly lost on:** pausing but never resuming. A notebook that fires the
interrupt and stops — often with the resume call left commented out — proves
half the requirement. This is the most frequent half-finished deliverable of
all.

### 6. LangGraph functional API & error handling — 15 pts

**Where:** [Thinking in LangGraph](09_langgraph.qmd) ·
[Workflow patterns](10_workflows.ipynb) · [Reliability](13_reliability.qmd)

**Full marks:** built with `@task` / `@entrypoint`, plus **at least two** of the
four error strategies implemented in code.

**Commonly lost on:** two things. First, building on `StateGraph` — it works,
but the rubric names the **Functional API** specifically. Second, a
hand-written `for` loop with `time.sleep()` presented as "transient retry"; the
requirement is a real `RetryPolicy` object.

### 7. Workflow pattern — 10 pts

**Where:** [Workflow patterns](10_workflows.ipynb)

**Full marks:** implement one of Prompt Chaining, Parallelization, Routing,
Orchestrator-Worker, or Evaluator-Optimizer — and **name it** in your write-up,
with a sentence on why it fits.

**Commonly lost on:** implementing one correctly and never naming it. The
points are for the explicit choice, so say the words.

### 8. LangSmith observability — 5 pts

**Where:** [LangSmith](11_langsmith.qmd) · [LangSmith lab](14_langsmith_lab.qmd)

**Full marks:** tracing genuinely on, plus a short write-up of something the
trace actually showed you — a bottleneck, a bad tool call, a retry firing.

**Commonly lost on:** the variable name. It is `LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2`.
`LANGSMITH_TRACING_V2` is not a real variable: it fails silently, produces no
trace, and no error. Verify your key before your demo, not after.

## GitHub & documentation requirements

These apply to **every project in every SDAIA Academy programme**, on top of the
eight sections above, and they are part of how the project is evaluated — not
paperwork. Your repository must include:

- A clear, comprehensive **project description**
- A **professional README** — the project idea, plus how to run and use it
- Proper **technical documentation**
- Good **Git practices** — meaningful, incremental commits, a sane structure,
  and a `.gitignore` that excludes secrets and generated files
- A statement of **which training programme** the project was completed under
  (programme name + cohort dates)
- A link to **[SDAIA Academy's GitHub](https://github.com/SDAIAAcademy)** where
  relevant

Every trainee needs an active GitHub account, and projects are expected to stay
documented and updated there.

*Encouraged, not scored:* star and follow strong Saudi repositories and
accounts, contribute to open source, engage through forks, pull requests and
issues, and share standout projects with the community.

## The write-up

One short paragraph per section, saying which pattern you used and why. This is
how understanding is verified, and it is worth real marks on its own.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Write it from your results, not from your plan
Graders check the write-up against the code and the captured output. Claims
that contradict your own notebook are worse than an admitted gap — and they are
easy to spot. Two real examples:

- A write-up stating the trace "confirmed low latency" in a notebook whose own
  output shows `403 Forbidden` on every tracing attempt.
- A write-up describing a full working pipeline in a repo where every cell is
  unexecuted and the documents are still placeholder text.

If something did not work, say so and describe what you inspected instead. An
honest gap costs a few points. A claim your own output contradicts costs
credibility across the whole submission.
:::

## Before you submit

- [ ] **Your full name is in the README or the notebook header.** Submissions
      without names are not graded — this is not a formality.
- [ ] Restart the kernel and **run everything top to bottom.** Fresh, in order.
- [ ] Every demo cell has **captured output** saved in the file.
- [ ] The interrupt **and** the resume both ran.
- [ ] A cross-thread test proves long-term memory.
- [ ] No API key in the code or in git history.
- [ ] No `TODO` or template placeholder text left anywhere.
- [ ] Your declared track (A / B / C / D) is stated explicitly.
- [ ] Every claim in the write-up is backed by something visible in the file.
- [ ] **README** covers the project description and how to run it, `.gitignore`
      excludes secrets, and the programme name and cohort dates are stated.
